posts.content:
I've been thinking about writing down my thoughts for years.

I've started, and abandoned, more blogs than I care to admit. I always convinced myself my ideas weren't fully formed enough to share. They needed to be clearer. The argument needed to be tighter. The "so what?" needed to be actionable.

Then I attended my second Future of Software event (FOSE).

One thing struck me more than anything else. The most valuable conversations weren't polished conclusions. They were half formed ideas, observations, patterns people were starting to notice, and questions nobody had the answers to yet.

It made me realize that my job isn't to write about answers we already know, it's to spot patterns, explore possibilities, and ask better questions before the answers are obvious.

I watched so many people come back from FOSE, publish their early thinking, and invite others into the conversation. It made me ask myself: why do I feel I have to wait until everything is perfect?

So, as a recovering perfectionist, I'm giving myself permission to think out loud. That's why I'm calling this series Rachel's Ramblings.

Some posts will genuinely be rambles. Others may be more fully formed. But calling them ramblings gives me permission to publish both, instead of waiting until every sentence is perfect.

Martin Fowler has been encouraging (or perhaps gently nudging!) me to do this for quite a while. I've finally decided that, with so much uncertainty and transformation happening across our industry, now feels like exactly the right time to start.

The first Rambling is simply why I'm doing this. The next one, coming soon, is about how the role of the software developer is changing.

I'd love to hear what resonates, what you disagree with, and what you're seeing too.

posts.content:
As we move further into agentic systems, I think we're going to have to get much more sophisticated about how we think about models.

Not every task an agent performs needs frontier-level intelligence. Some steps need deep reasoning. Others are high-volume, repetitive or very specific to your business. Using the biggest, most capable model for every one of those steps isn't necessarily the best architecture, and the economics certainly won't make sense at scale.

Our teams have been experimenting with NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to understand what a more specialized model approach could look like. What I found interesting was how quickly they could adapt the model to a particular domain, change how it behaves without meaningfully degrading its broader capabilities, and significantly improve inference speed.
For me, the bigger story isn't really about one model. It's that agentic AI is increasingly going to be a system of models, and we're going to need to make deliberate choices about which model does which job.

That changes the enterprise AI question from "which is the best model?" to something much more interesting: where do we actually need frontier intelligence, and where would greater control, specialization and better economics produce a better system?

Gustavo A. Lujan, Allen Roush and Andy Nolan share what they learned, and all the technical detail, here: https://lnkd.in/e5qFhqFN

posts.content:
Yesterday at Code Remix Summit I spoke about two sides of the AI transition that are deeply connected, but too often discussed separately.

First: the human side of AI with Kiran Rouzie
We spend enormous energy talking about model capability, benchmarks, tooling and agentic workflows. What we don’t talk about enough is how people’s roles are changing, what new skills matter most, and how leaders create engagement instead of fear.

Adoption is not the metric. Engagement is.

The organizations that will get disproportionate value from AI are the ones that unlock the creativity, judgment and curiosity of their people. That requires investment in learning, experimentation, trust and new ways of working, not just new tooling.

Second: I joined a panel with leaders from Dov B. Katz from Morgan Stanley, Anshuman Chadha from Uber, Jonathan Schneider from Moderne, Dr. Harald Aamot from SAP and Brian Houck from DX discussing escalating token and verification costs.

And honestly, panels are only interesting when there’s genuine diversity of ideas, experiences and opinions. This one definitely delivered that with one theme everyone is now starting to wrestle with: code review at scale in an AI-assisted world.

My answer? Pair programming and CI, but I’ll save the full rant on that for another day.

My view is that harness engineering will unlock a huge amount of value over the next phase of AI adoption. We need to bring engineering discipline to how we build with agents:
• clearer context management
• better orchestration
• stronger evaluation patterns
• deterministic checks and guardrails where appropriate
• using smaller and non-frontier models intentionally

Not every problem needs the most powerful model. Good engineering decisions matter.

I’ve said this many times: organizations with strong XP and engineering foundations are handling the explosion in generated code, verification demands and cost management far better than those without disciplined software delivery practices underneath them.

AI does not reduce the need for engineering discipline. It increases it.

The next phase of advantage will not come from who experiments the fastest.
It will come from who can scale quality, trust, engagement and cost control at the same time.

posts.content:
Matt Shumer’s piece this week went viral for a reason. He’s right, AI is advancing quickly and the impact on work is real. 

What’s missing from much of the conversation, though, is nuance. We’re not simply watching humans get replaced. We’re watching the nature of valuable work change. The next category of work isn’t just about generating output, it’s about orchestrating systems, verifying results and applying judgment when context really matters.

Most of the flashy examples focus on greenfield projects. But the real economic weight of most organizations sits in brownfield environments, legacy estates, regulated systems and decades of institutional knowledge. That’s where AI applied thoughtfully can have outsized impact. Not by blindly rewriting everything, but by helping us understand, analyze and evolve what already exists.

There’s also a growing gap between what AI can do and what we can confidently secure and govern. Closing that gap will separate serious operators from casual experimenters.

So yes, push AI into your work. But don’t stop at prompting. Learn to orchestrate. Lean into complexity. Build expertise in governance and risk. And double down on judgment and empathy, because those are not easily automated.

This will be a defining period. The advantage will go to those who combine curiosity with discipline and move forward with both ambition and responsibility.

It was candid, provocative and energizing in equal measure. There are no clear answers right now, which made the unconference format exactly right. The staff engineer role is shifting toward orchestration and governance of agents. We need to rethink code reviews and testing in a world where much of the code is generated, possibly tiering software by risk and strengthening guardrails in the pipeline. We also discussed agent topologies, safer programming models, and the potential for self-healing systems supported by a unified ledger of change across logic, infrastructure and data.

This year I’ll be digging further into cognitive debt mitigation, human-in-the-loop design, verification over inspection, and what a practical “agent subconscious” could look like in production environments. We are at a starting point. Strategy now means forming hypotheses, running experiments and learning quickly. I’m looking forward to sharing what we discover as we put these ideas into practice.

posts.content:
It’s been just over a week since I was at the NYC CIO Executive Summit, and I’ve been reflecting on the conversations since.

One clear takeaway stood out. The early promises of efficiency gains from GenAI have not materialized for most organizations. What leaders are seeing instead is improvement at the individual and team level, better effectiveness rather than step-change cost reduction. As a result, the conversation has shifted from cost cutting to value creation.

That’s where the tension sits.

Technology leaders know they can’t afford to be left behind. They need their teams to upskill. They need to invest in new ways of creating value. And yet, many are being asked to cut budgets, not grow them.

There was a real hope that efficiency gains would fund the next wave of investment. For most, that funding hasn’t shown up.

So this is the struggle:
- We must invest, but we have very little room to do so.
- We know this is a major change program, but the end state isn’t as clear as it was during earlier digital transformation journeys.
- And many leaders aren’t sure where to start.

Challenging, ambiguous, and consequential.
 
Interesting times indeed.

posts.content:
TL;DR: AI is changing software engineering jobs faster than most organizations are changing how they develop talent. Leaders need to act now, not later.

The long version:
AI dominated the business and technology conversation in 2025. Most of that debate focused on productivity. Far less attention has been paid to what AI means for people, skills and careers. That’s an area that needs much more attention in 2026.

In this piece, Joanna Parke and I argue that the biggest risk isn’t whether AI makes teams faster today, but whether we are creating the talent, knowledge and cultures we’ll need in five years’ time. Ignore that, and you end up with skills gaps, weak succession planning and fragile engineering cultures.
We’re already seeing a shift from writing code to orchestrating systems. Engineers are becoming stewards of reliability, performance and value, working alongside AI rather than competing with it. This is where the idea of the “expert generalist” really matters: people who deeply understand systems, fundamentals and failure modes, not just syntax.

That makes how we grow talent critical. Junior engineers are increasingly AI-native, but foundational skills still matter. Leaders have a responsibility to ensure new developers learn how software really works, where AI helps, and where it doesn’t. Training alone isn’t enough; mentorship, pairing and collaborative learning are becoming strategic capabilities.

We also explore whether it’s time to rethink apprenticeship models and professional standards in software engineering. That may sound radical, but AI is creating real questions of accountability and authority, and the industry needs an answer.

This isn’t about resisting change. It’s about shaping it deliberately.
If software has eaten the world, then how we develop the next generation of engineers is no longer a side issue. It’s a leadership issue.

posts.content:
Enterprise modernization isn’t failing because of retiring programmers. It’s failing because of a leadership disconnect.

Legacy systems work. That’s exactly why senior leaders see modernization as unnecessary risk and why younger technologists see legacy firms as career dead ends. The result is paralysis.

In this piece, we argue the standoff is rational on both sides and show how new, incremental, behavior-led modernization approaches, now accelerated by generative AI, change the risk equation entirely.
Modernization no longer has to be a career-defining gamble. It can be incremental, provable, and reversible.

If you want to know more, check out this piece in InformationWeek, that I cowrote with Edward Hieatt, COO at Mechanical Orchard.

Would love to hear how others are navigating this challenge.

posts.content:
Day 2 of Radar, and it’s great to see so many familiar faces alongside new ones.

We’ve already covered a lot of ground. The rapid rise of agent coding assistants. The new workflow tooling emerging to support agent-driven development. The economics of tokens and what that means for real-world engineering decisions.

We’ve also talked about something critical: managing disposable code as disposable, and treating durable code very differently. Not everything generated by an agent deserves the same lifecycle, governance, or investment.

And importantly, we can’t forget everything we’ve learned about building resilient, distributed systems just because we’re now building agents. Reliability, observability, fault tolerance, and clear system boundaries still matter. In many cases, they matter more.

The technology is evolving quickly. The fundamentals still apply.

posts.content:
The second Rachel's Rambling is now live on Martin Fowler's website.

Over the last year we've been obsessed with productivity.

How well can an LLM write code?
How much faster can we build software?
How do we verify AI-generated code?
How do we ensure it's well designed, secure and resilient?

Those are all important questions, but I wonder if we've been so focused on the mechanics of AI that we've missed one of the biggest shifts happening underneath.

Leadership has always been about energy management. Whether you're a CTO, an architect or a developer, your value isn't measured by how much work you personally produce. It's measured by where you choose to invest your finite attention and judgement.

As AI takes on more of the implementation, that's becoming true for developers too. The next big challenge may not be whether we can direct and verify AI at scale. It may be whether we can manage our own energy well enough to consistently exercise good judgement at scale.

That shift in thinking is what led me to compare the role of a developer to that of an orchestra conductor. Less about playing every instrument. More about deciding where your attention has the greatest impact.

I'd love to hear whether this resonates.

Five months ago, many of the conversations about AI and software development still felt broad and uncertain. At our latest Future of Software Development Retreat, the questions felt much more practical.

We’re now talking about harnesses, team shapes, developer roles, agentic development and what the SDLC needs to become next.

There’s no single answer yet, and that’s okay. What I’m seeing is a lot of thoughtful experimentation across legacy systems, infrastructure and product development.

For me, the most important thing is to return to first principles: why do our practices exist, what feedback loops do they create and where do they need to evolve?

I remain optimistic about the future of software development. Engineering judgment, design and architecture still matter deeply, especially as we build systems that need to be resilient, adaptable and cost-effective in an AI-native world.

Sharing a few reflections from the retreat.

posts.content:
It’s hard to keep up with everything happening in tech at the moment. That’s not because there’s too little content but because there’s way too much. The challenge is figuring out what actually matters.

That’s partly why I’m starting a quarterly newsletter, From the CTO. It’s a space to share what I’m noticing, the questions I’m sitting with and the shifts I think leaders should be paying attention to.

Earlier this year, we got a group of practitioners together in Utah (hosted by Martin Fowler) to talk about the future of software engineering.

One idea stuck with me: engineering rigor won’t ever disappear, but it will move elsewhere. The question is ‘where?’

As AI starts generating more code, the work of building software will likely change:

from writing → to validating
from output → to judgment
from speed → to decision-making

At the same time, new tensions are emerging: teams are shipping faster, but decisions aren’t keeping pace and while productivity appears to be up developer experience is arguably degrading.

This first edition digs into some of that, taking in “supervisory engineering” and what leaders need to rethink around governance and security.

There are no big conclusions yet: it’s vital, though, to start making sense of the signal.

I’m curious how others are navigating this, so please let me know in the comments! 👇
